lead: A two-qubit gate changes two qubits at once, and that is what lets a circuit create entanglement — something no single-qubit gate can do. CNOT flips a target qubit only when its control qubit is 1, and it is the workhorse for making Bell pairs. SWAP exchanges two qubits and is built from three CNOTs. The Toffoli gate adds a second control, so it flips its target only when both controls are 1 — the key to reversible classical logic. Unit 4 algorithms and Unit 5 protocols are assembled from these gates.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for single-qubit gates and their 2×2 matrices, and the Unit 2 chapter on tensor-product order and Bell states.

blocks.text: A controlled gate acts on a target qubit only when a control qubit is in state |1⟩. The control itself is never changed. When the control is |0⟩ the gate does nothing to the target. This one rule turns any single-qubit gate into a two-qubit gate.
CNOT means controlled-NOT, also called controlled-X. Let a be the control bit and b the target bit. CNOT flips b when a = 1, and leaves b alone when a = 0.

blocks.where: a is the control bit (0 or 1), b is the target bit, and ⊕ is XOR, that is addition mod 2. So b ⊕ a equals b when a = 0, and equals 1 − b when a = 1.
Rows and columns follow the order |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩, with the first qubit as the control. The matrix leaves |00⟩ and |01⟩ unchanged and exchanges |10⟩ with |11⟩.

blocks.text: CNOT is its own inverse: applying it twice gives b ⊕ a ⊕ a = b, so the input returns. In a circuit diagram the control is a dot and the target is ⊕, joined by a vertical line. With the target starting at 0, CNOT copies the control bit into the target — the standard trick for computing parity in error correction.

SWAP exchanges two qubits: |a, b⟩ → |b, a⟩. It has no control qubit and no target — both qubits are treated equally. Its 4×4 matrix is the identity except that the rows for |01⟩ and |10⟩ are exchanged.

items: Apply CNOT with control 1, target 2: the pair becomes (a, a ⊕ b).
Apply CNOT with control 2, target 1: the new first bit is a ⊕ (a ⊕ b) = b, giving (b, a ⊕ b).
Apply CNOT with control 1, target 2 again: the new second bit is (a ⊕ b) ⊕ b = a, giving (b, a).

blocks.text: The order matters: the middle gate points the other way. Two CNOTs do not swap; three do. SWAP is also its own inverse, because swapping twice restores the input. Hardware that lacks a native SWAP simply runs this three-gate sequence.
The Toffoli gate, or CCNOT, uses three qubits: two controls a and b, and one target c. It flips c only when a and b are both 1.

blocks.where: a and b are the control bits, c is the target bit, and a · b is the AND of the two controls (1 only when both are 1).

blocks.text: Only the last two rows change, so the 8×8 matrix is the identity with |110⟩ and |111⟩ exchanged. With the target starting at 0, Toffoli computes AND of the two controls. Combined with NOT it gives NAND, and NAND alone builds any classical circuit — so Toffoli makes classical logic reversible. That is why adders and oracles in Unit 4 are drawn with Toffoli gates.

A related gate some syllabi list next to Toffoli is the Fredkin gate, or controlled-SWAP: a third qubit decides whether two target qubits are exchanged. It is reversible and never changes the number of 1s in the register.

sections.h3: H followed by CNOT makes a Bell state

blocks.text: Start with two qubits in |00⟩. Apply H to the first qubit, using the gate from 3.1.

items: Apply CNOT with control 1 and target 2.
In the |00⟩ term the control is 0, so the target stays 0.
In the |10⟩ term the control is 1, so the target flips from 0 to 1, giving |11⟩.
Final state: (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, which is the Bell state |Φ⁺⟩.

blocks.text: Before the CNOT the state is a product of two separate qubit states. After it, no product form exists: the qubits are entangled, and measuring one tells you the other. A single CNOT achieves this only because H first put the control into a superposition of 0 and 1. The same H-then-CNOT recipe prepares the Bell pair used in 3.6 and 3.7.

figure.caption: The worked example follows |01⟩ through CNOT(1→2), CNOT(2→1), CNOT(1→2): (q1,q2) goes (0,1) → (0,1) → (1,1) → (1,0). The middle gate reverses the control, and the final |10⟩ is |01⟩ with its two bits swapped.

spec.title: SWAP worked example
spec.aria: A five-step left-to-right chain follows the basis state |01⟩ through CNOT(1→2), CNOT(2→1) and CNOT(1→2), ending at |10⟩.

examples.question: Start with the two-qubit state |01⟩, that is q1 = 0 and q2 = 1. Apply CNOT(1→2), then CNOT(2→1), then CNOT(1→2). Give the state after each gate as the bit values (q1, q2), and state the final state. Does this sequence swap the two qubits?
steps: CNOT(1→2): control q1 = 0, so the target q2 is not flipped. q2 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. State is |01⟩ with q1 = 0, q2 = 1.
CNOT(2→1): control q2 = 1, so flip q1. q1 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. State is |11⟩ with q1 = 1, q2 = 1.
CNOT(1→2): control q1 = 1, so flip q2. q2 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. State is |10⟩ with q1 = 1, q2 = 0.
The input was |01⟩ (q1 = 0, q2 = 1) and the output is |10⟩ (q1 = 1, q2 = 0). The two bits have exchanged places.
examples.answer: The final state is |10⟩ with q1 = 1 and q2 = 0, which is the input |01⟩ with its two qubits swapped.
examples.check:
q1, q2 = 0, 1
q2 = q2 ^ q1
print(q1)
print(q2)
q1 = q1 ^ q2
print(q1)
print(q2)
q2 = q2 ^ q1
print(q1)
print(q2)

traps: CNOT is not SWAP. CNOT keeps the control fixed and may flip only the target; SWAP exchanges both qubits.

Two CNOTs in opposite directions do not swap. You need three, and the middle one must point opposite to the other two: 1→2, 2→1, 1→2 swaps, and so does 2→1, 1→2, 2→1 (the same circuit with the qubit labels exchanged). Three CNOTs all pointing the same way do not swap.
Toffoli fires only when both controls are 1. It does not fire when either one is 1 — that would be a different gate.

Fix the basis order before writing a matrix. With |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩ and the first qubit as control, CNOT exchanges |10⟩ and |11⟩; if the target comes first, the matrix looks different. State your convention in the answer.
A CNOT whose control is |0⟩ does nothing to the target. Many answers wrongly flip the target anyway.

quiz.q: Write the action of CNOT with control q1 and target q2 on the basis state |10⟩.
quiz.a: q1 = 1 so the target flips: q2 goes from 0 to 1, giving |11⟩.

quiz.q: How many CNOT gates build a SWAP, and in which directions are they applied?
quiz.a: Three: CNOT(1→2), then CNOT(2→1), then CNOT(1→2).

quiz.q: Explain why CNOT is its own inverse, using the formula b → b ⊕ a.
quiz.a: Applying CNOT twice gives b ⊕ a ⊕ a. Since a ⊕ a = 0, the result is b ⊕ 0 = b, the original target. The control is never changed. So U_CNOT · U_CNOT = I.

quiz.q: Start from |00⟩. Apply H to q1, then CNOT(1→2). Give the final state and name it.
quiz.a: H on q1 gives (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 on q1 and |0⟩ on q2, so the state is (|00⟩ + |10⟩)/√2. CNOT flips q2 only in the |10⟩ term, giving (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. That is the Bell state |Φ⁺⟩.

quiz.q: A Toffoli gate has controls a, b and target c. Give the output for the inputs |110⟩ and |101⟩.
quiz.a: For |110⟩ both controls are 1, so c flips from 0 to 1: output |111⟩. For |101⟩ the second control is 0, so a·b = 0 and c is unchanged: output |101⟩.

quiz.q: A student replaces the three-CNOT SWAP with the two gates CNOT(1→2) then CNOT(2→1) and claims the qubits are swapped. Test the claim on the input |01⟩ and explain what went wrong.
quiz.a: CNOT(1→2) on |01⟩ does nothing (control 0), giving q1 = 0, q2 = 1. CNOT(2→1) flips q1 because q2 = 1, giving |11⟩. The output is |11⟩, not the swapped |10⟩. The third CNOT is what restores the second bit, so two gates are not enough.

beyond: Not for the exam. Toffoli and Fredkin gates are the centre of reversible computing, a line of work that studies how to run classical logic without erasing bits, since erasing a bit has a thermodynamic cost. Real hardware rarely offers a native three-qubit gate, so compilers break Toffoli into CNOTs and single-qubit rotations, and the count of those CNOTs is a standard cost measure for adders and oracle circuits. Search for reversible logic synthesis, the Margolus gate, or the Qiskit multi-controlled-X instruction to see how this is done in practice.
